newsitem.title: USA: GM's Chevrolet optimistic about Venture sales.
newsitem.headline: GM's Chevrolet optimistic about Venture sales.

text.p: General Motors Corp expects to sell between 70,000 and 75,000 of its new Chevrolet Venture minivans in 1997 after the vehicles go on sale in February or March, the division's general manager said Monday.

John Middlebrook, general manager of Chevrolet, GM's largest single division, said dealers should have "good availability of the products when advertising begins, although he warned overall inventories will be tight.
"We're going to be short because I think demand will exceed supply," Middlebrook told reporters following a speech at the 1997 Automotive News World Congress.

Middlebrook said the Venture launch is on schedule at GM's plant in Doraville, Ga. GM has had major problems in the past launching new vehicles. It has provided little to no specific information about the Doraville start-up, which includes several other minivan models for both the U.S. and overseas.

Despite flat total U.S. minivan sales during the last several months, Middlebrook predicted the segment will grow 25 percent over the next five years as buyers from more demographic groups need the practicality they offer.
Last week, Toyota Motor Corp executives said they expect to sell all of the 50,000 to 60,000 new Sienna minivans they can produce in the first model year it is on the market.

In his remarks, Middlebrook outlined several initiatives the division is taking to focus more on customer needs and improve customer loyalty and satisfaction -- the area he called the industry's goal into the next century. The division plans a national roll-out of what it calls brand critical standards later this year.

For instance, the division will expand its "Custom XPress Delivery" system for the Blazer to other areas. A pilot program in place in California has had good results. Under the program, dealers aim to provide next day delivery on popularly configured models by using a regional distribution center.

Chevrolet is also working to slashing the time it takes to purchase a new vehicle to 90 minutes from the six to eight hours it often takes. Middlebrook said Chevrolet is also pressing dealers to spend 80 percent of their time counseling buyers and 20 percent haggling over the price -- instead of the usual process now in which those two numbers are reversed.
Chevrolet is continuing its plan to reduce the number of dealerships. Eventually, the division wants 4,000 in the U.S. instead of the current 4,400.
"Today, building a quality product is just the price of entry. Dealership experiences set us apart and help make the difference between winning and losing a loyal customer," he said.
